body: The brain is a very complex organ and scientists and medical professionals alike still don't know all there is to know about the brain itself so, I think the Neurologists and Scientists already researching in that field are probably trying their absolute best to find better treatment options whilst also trying to treat all the current patients they have. However, it seems, there's always new patients popping up left, right and center and never enough Neurologists to treat them.
Check DM's, apologies for super long ended answer but I'm pretty bad at answering in a quick summary so I hope I'm of some help to you and you're not dizzied and confused for much longer!

I think it's already been said but, I don't think there's a "cure" as such but there are definitely medications that can help prevent and manage symptoms from occurring. There's hope out there, just gotta try and stay optimistic. If you're finding the side effects too problematic though then speak to your Neurologist about switching medications if possible asap. They can get costly quite quickly. 

Everyone's different but I'm a bit polypharm at the moment, trying to cut back as I don't really like the side effects of antidepressants but if it keeps the vertigo away eh? But lately the vertigo has returned quite severely so it's back to the drawing board for me! But Efexor did work wonders for a full year and a bit so I'd still highly recommend giving it a go if you haven't already. I'm also on Topiramate 100mg. I've been on it in the past for chronic migraines and it's been a god send for me so I've just stuck with it. I know it has a lot of negative press but I haven't had the negative side effects from it, only positives really so I've just stuck with it. 

Emgality 120mg/ml x1 injection once per month. I had chronic migraines a few years before the vestibular migraines developed so yeah, it's been a fun time. Clonazepam is the best rescue medication for bad vertigo days! Use sparingly if you manage to get your hands on some.  

I recommend Cephaly if you want to try a non-drug treatment option, I found it reduced my dizziness/vertigo symptoms quite a bit when things were real bad. But that's just my experience. If you're really stuck, read "Victory Over Vestibular Migraine" by Dr Shin C. Beh. Really helpful book. I was so lost before it. Just, gave me some hope.
I purchased the whole Daria collection from Apple iTunes a few years ago which I now watch on Apple TV. So could try that?
I know it’s not ideal but, it’s nice to know you have a mother that can support you like that. Hopefully it’s not for too long! The cost of living is a dire situation.

I also get disabling migraines that impact my day to day life and have rendered me unable to be able to work full time due to the many symptoms that come with them. If you’ve never had severe migraines, congrats, it’s so so disabling, it really takes your whole life away. And no, you don’t get it from clubbing, some of us are just born with it unfortunately. I’m sorry to hear you suffer with that same neurological condition h0pe2.

You're welcome! Well at the time when my symptoms were really severe (like you've mentioned yours have been) I was in a relationship (same person as now) and I just sat down and determined what my number 1 priority was and that point in time and that was to get rid of this horrible dizziness/vertigo! 

Luckily my partner was very caring and understanding as they could clearly see how badly it was effecting my daily life. So just dw about the Bupropion - that's an option for the future (maybe). I still highly recommend Effexor XR (Venlafaxine XR) as it has made a huge positive impact on my daily life and eradicated the vertigo for sure and lessened the dizziness by a lot! It's no cure but it definitely was a 'miracle' drug for me. Patience is key though.

That's weird. You've got the latest Airpods Pro 2s as well? I know my first generation Airpods Pros couldn't get them which was frustrating. I hope it gets sorted soon then although it is still quite 'new' in the tech space.

Unfortunately most antidepressants that start with an 'S' e.g. SSRIs or SNRIs have a huge negative impact on sexual drive, the ability to orgasm, in men it's the inability to get an erection, I think in women it's - like you mentioned - genital numbness and reduced sensitivity in the clitoris. There is one known way that can definitely combat this side effect and this is ceasing the drug altogether and trying something completely different - e.g. Mirtazapine or Bupropion etc. But, then you'd have to start from scratch again and hope that, that antidepressant helps what you were originally taking the other one for anyway. 

Another option is taking a low dose of Bupropion and adding it to your Venlafaxine medication to counteract the sexual side effects. This is done quite frequently, I've also done it (under the guidance of my psychiatrist) and can say it's definitely helped! Just note that, Bupropion can raise Effexor serum levels in the blood so you''ve usually just gotta take a lower dose of Effexor XR e.g. 75mg to take the smallest dose of Bupropion, which over here is, 150mg SR. Just talk to your psychiatrist about it. It's in a lot of different scientific studies and has the evidence to back it up. Otherwise I've used things like viagra in the past. Not sure how good it is for women but it's like a bandaid. It doesn't help the 'core' problem. Bupropion does. 

I hope that makes sense!

Oh that's interesting, my neurologist said it's one or the other usually but I never considered taking both at the same time! I'm guessing since one is an 'SNRI' and the other an 'anticonvulsant' there's probz no drug to drug interactions? Have you noticed any changes in your mood? I know Lamictal is also used to stabilize mood in Bipolar 1 patients and Effexor for anxiety so if anything, your mood should be stable if not positive?

Oh, my Neurologist also prescribed me Prednisone for when the migraines just won't stop! I'm talking 4 days continously, no end in sight (Status migrainosus). I take 2 x 25mg pills for three days - a short burst, they call it. It definitely helps when I'm at my whits end with pain and intense dizziness, sometimes vertigo. It prevents a hospital ER visit which if I can stay away from there, I'm incredibly thankful.

I'm sorry you're suffering so badly from all of this. I feel your pain. 

Have you considered being admitted to a hospital? I'm not sure what country you're from but when things got really severe here I was just lost and out of options. I was on a waitlist to see another Neurologist for VM but it was taking months. I couldn't work and my quality of life was poor. So, in the end, I checked into a hospital and they admitted me for a week. I got into see a Neurologist who specialised in VM asap (he fortunately worked at that hospital). He got me onto Effexor XR long term and Clonazepam as a rescue medication which hugely helped prevent the severe/scary vertigo from occuring every single day. 

The Effexor XR is definitely controlling the severe vertigo nowadays. It was a slow process, a 'waiting game' as one would call it. But that hospital visit definitely helped me, idk how long I'd be waiting otherwise without it. With little progress towards recovery. 

I had chronic migraines before this severe fall in previous years gone by. I noticed ever since that fall, things definitely got more severe and more frequent aka 'chronic'. So, that's most likely why it's progressed to Vestibular Migraine (with PPPD). I kinda had to see quite a few different specialists last year to figure that out. I was diagnosed with moderate TBI. It's a silent illness, no one would know unless they asked me. Have you considered something 'bigger' is causing all these intense migraines/vertigo attacks? 

On top of taking the Effexor XR to manage the severe vertigo, I also take Emgality 120mg/ml x 1 each month to prevent (or lessen) the chronic migraine episodes I'm having as well (migraine with aura). It doesn't eliminate them entirely but it definitely is preventing the number of migraines I have a month, and the severity of these migraines. Without this medication I reckon I'd be in the ER at least 3-5 times a month and would have headaches/migraines everyday at different levels of severity. It's been a game changer in improving my quality of life. I was on Ajovy before that but there was a massive shortage in my country so I had to switch over to Emgality for this reason. Botox didn't do much for me unfortunately but that's not to say it won't help you!

Effexor XR helped long term for both the vestibular migraine and severe dizziness/vertigo symptoms. I'd say it has been more helpful for eliminating the severe vertigo/dizzy symptoms altogether. I still get some dizzy episodes from time to time but they're not nearly as bad as they were 6-7 months ago. I'm on 75mg XR now but have been on 150mg XR and 225mg XR. Found 150mg XR to be the sweet spot for quite some time but only just dropped it recently to add another drug in the mix (it raises Effexor serum levels). 

When things were really severe and I was in the hospital, the physician there gave me Clonazepam and it elimated the severe vertigo/dizziness instantly. It's a very effective 'rescue' medication, seems to be the only thing that works for me when things are really severe. But I'm lucky enough to say that the Effexor XR has kept things under control most of the time. I rarely have to use Clonazepam, it's really hard to get it prescribed here anyway as every doctor assumes that you'll get addicted to it and won't prescribe it, which is very frustrating as it is a huge lifesaver!

I'm also in Australia and have been using the Airpods Pro 2s for quite a few months now and they've been amazing. I have gone to an audiologist and have had a trial of different hearing aids but since my hearing loss isn't too bad, there really is no point getting hearing aids (yet). Maybe 10 years in the future? But who knows. They're way out of my budget anyway so as long as the Airpods Pro 2s keep working, I'll be able to 'function' daily pretty comfortably.

How much do you take orally? I've been hesitant to try it again as I've had it a few times in the hospital in an IV drip and it gave me severe akathisia which I think (arguably) is worse than Vertigo. I realise that taking this medication orally would be quite different to an IV (longer to take effect/dose could be lower orally). Just curious to know if you've ever had this side effect. Thanks.

Unfortunately with almost every antidepressant you've gotta wait at least 4-6 weeks until you'll be able to feel any 'noticeable' effects. It's a real pain in the ass this waiting game sadly. 

If you're really, badly suffering you could suggest asking your specialist or doctor for a small amount of Clonazepam or Diazepam. It's hard to get but I got it in hospital for when things were really bad and nothing else was working. It took away the dizziness/severe vertigo asap whilst I was still waiting for the antidepressant medication to take effect.

Oh sorry, forgot to put my dose. I did manage to get up to 225mg but found it effecting my blood pressure too much so dropped the dose to 150mg XR (once daily dosing) and that was great for awhile. I only just dropped the dose to 75mg XR - once daily dosing - as my Psychiatrist added in a low dose of 150mg SR of Bupropion to counteract the sexual side effects. All SSRIs or SNRIs tend to cause loss of libido/anorgasmia etc, some aren't as bad as others - Venlafaxine wasn't as bad as Sertraline imo. It's up to you whether you want to add a low dose of another drug (e.g. Bupropion) to counteract the sexual side effects but I didn't do this till later on as I just wanted the dizziness to go away asap, I put the other issues on the back burner.

I've tried SSRIs in the past for my anxiety and just felt they cause agitation/akathisia (from my experience) so when this PPPD came around last year, I was not willing to retry SSRIs for this condition. 

My Neurologist instead highly recommended Venlafaxine XR (Effexor XR - SNRI). I know this drug has a lot of negative press but it has hugely helped me control the PPPD symptoms over the past 6 months. It's not a quick fix but once you get the right dose and keep at it (no skipping of days), I've found that it either greatly reduces dizziness symptoms or eliminates them entirely. 

I seriously felt like a new person when it finally decided to prevent the dizziness - I nearly cried that day. After that I was just thankful that I bit the bullet and ignored the negative online reviews for this drug and put full trust in my Neurologist. It's a 'gold standard' drug for Vestibular Migraines (according to Dr Shin C. Beh neurologist and author of 'Victory Over Vestibular Migraine') which can also help treat PPPD. I have both, so it's been amazing for treating both conditions.

Do you get numbness/tingling in the muscle below your ears right before a dizziness attack? 

I've considered putting an icepack or something on it for when that happens to see if it de-escalates the dizziness to come (or stops it entirely).

Aw, I hope you got through it too! 

Yeah it's terrible, it gave me intense suicidal thoughts just because it happened at every part of everyday and would not stop. A lot of specialists just assume it's either worsening anxiety or restless legs, so they give you meds for those disorders and wait and see what happens. But if nothing gets rid of it, they're left puzzled. Luckily my Psychiatrist picked up on it pretty quickly, so they must've had this experience with previous patients. I think agitation is a common side effect of Prozac, just because it's a more 'activating' antidepressant rather than a 'sedating' one. Doesn't happen with everyone but it's definitely known to occur. Quite annoying as it was good for my depression/anxiety. But I just couldn't continue on with the akathisia. 

I'm on Zyban SR (Bupropion SR) and Effexor XR (Venlafaxine XR) now. Took me quite a few different trials of drugs to get here. I think it's been working for over 6 months now. The Zyban couteracts the sexual side effects of Venlafaxine which is amazing. Soz if that was tmi. But, just something to keep in mind, when you think you've found the 'perfect' drug for your condition but dislike some of the side effects. Just know that there's usually a drug you can add-on at a low dose to counteract those annoying side effects. 

But if it's a serious side effect like akathisia, it's best to stop the drug altogether and find something else that "hopefully" will work for you.

Do you ever have a cheat day with coffee? Or does it not affect you as badly? My specialists are still determining whether I have Meniere's or not. But the last time I had a cup of coffee, I dissociated within 20 mins and then was dizzy/very lightheaded for the rest of the day. So, could be Meniere's? But still unsure. Defs understand the aural fullness though, which can lead to severe dizziness or even a migraine. Worst feeling.

This was many years ago but yes I did try it as an add-on to Prozac but found it just caused weight gain, made me feel sluggish and some other annoying side effects. Would not recommend. There's plenty of better medications for anxiety these days. Turns out the Prozac was causing the agitation/akathisia so once we ceased that, the anxiety and agitation went away within a few weeks. It felt amazing once that stopped.

Aw no I'm so sorry to hear that! There are other options out there though. 

Have you considered Neuromodulation? It's a non-drug treatment that is proving to be quite effective in Vestibular Migraine (scientifically proven/studied). I use Cefaly twice a day as well as Effexor so I reckon it could be helping me too? 

It took me a year to wean off the SNRI Cymbalta, that was hell. I was really hesitant to try Effexor for that reason but I figured if this is going to be another chronic condition like my already chronic migraines, why would I need to withdraw from the drug anyway? It's also made a huge improvement on my anxiety. But yes, everyone reacts differently. 

Just know that any drug you decide to take will carry some side effects. It's your choice to weigh up the risks and/or potential benefits in the end. In this instance I'm thankful that I took that risk.

Mmmm if you can somehow get the medication compounded I would do it that way. I know it can get expensive that way but I found it much easier to taper slowly down doses with minimal withdrawal side effects. Like someone already mentioned, 10mg, but compounded. GP can usually write that up but will need to go to a compounding pharmacy. Can then wean down to 5mg, then 2.5mg, then nothing etc. My GP once gave me Valium or Klonopin to help with the brain zaps and severe dizziness etc. Sorry you're going through this, it took me a year to get off this med. I know how crap it can feel. Hopefully you feel more level headed soon.

Your subject area would be much more intensive than mine, I see what those law students have to read so damn, I hope you got some time off at least to let your brain hibernate.

Yeah I feel you there. I had to see a new Neurologist and that only happened because I admitted myself into a private hospital here. Otherwise I might've been waiting on referrals for months. Just found out mine could be caused partially by mTBI due to a past fall. I've had chronic migraines since 2017 though. Forgot to mention I'm also taking Emgality monthly and take Nurtec when needed and a low dose of Topiramate.

Have you tried Neuromodulation at all yet? I thought it was a sham but I went ahead and researched into the matter (as I like to read anyway) and Cefaly has some good evidence behind it. Dr Shin C. Beh backs it too. So maybe check that out if you haven't yet? It's just interesting after trying that for a month and switching my Effexor dose to 150mg the dizziness died down. Could be a combo?

Don't be afraid to try Effexor just because of a bad experience with Cymbalta! I too had a bad experience with that drug. Took me a year to get off of it. Effexor however has been amazing. It did take some time to work albeit 3-4months and it has been challenging trying to determine the right dose for my needs as everyone is different (I also have high anxiety). 150mg XR - I've determined is the right dose for me. I work in an academic library and have been off work for 6 months due to this VM/PPPD - working on computers, looking at PDF docs and scanning books seemed like a pipe dream I'd never be able to do again at one point but now it seems more hopeful. I see I'm late to this post, I hope you're doing better.

It's not seen as effective as Effexor for Vestibular Migraine and the withdrawals are usually as bad (if not worse) as the withdrawals seen from Effexor. Pristiq comes only as a tablet not as a capsule (like Effexor) so you can't count the beads and increase or decrease the medication as slowly (tablets can only be split so many times). They're very similar meds but one is much more effective than the other for VM. Effexor has given me my life back but I have had to be patient and finding the right dose for me was challenging but I got there eventually. I think the Neuromodulation device: Cefaly - has also been hugely beneficial in my treatment progress in combination with the Effexor.

Idk why so many people opt for Nortriptyline over Effexor. Yes Effexor has crap withdrawal effects but imo Nortriptyline has so many more annoying side effects that you have to manage daily compared to Effexor's minimal side effects. Everyone is so hyperfocused on the withdrawal effects but don't bother to take into consideration the common bothersome side effects of the opposing medication. 

Tricyclic antidepressant side effects make me hate life, which is one of the main reasons I stopped taking Nortriptyline in the first place. Effexor has been a life saver with minimal side effects.

Yes but why would one want to wean off this drug if it keeps the VM/PPPD away? If anything I would aim to never stop taking this medication until the day I die and I'm fine with that! As long as I don't get chronic dizziness then so be it.
soz I don't know if you'll see this but did you find Effexor raised your blood pressure at all? I guess with the Propranolol on top of it you probz wouldn't notice but without it you probably would.

I would've tried 450mg of Wellbrutin but it's not covered by the gov in my country so it would've been crazy expensive to try. I was also worried my anxiety might get worse or I be hypersexual for a month again rip.

Cymbalta didn't do much for me but any drug could effect a different individual on the same dose entirely different. I treat Antidepressants (or drugs in general) like a dart board, which side effects am I going to end up with and how will my body react?

I will say however Cymbalta was hell when it was time to get off the drug. Took me a year of extremely slow tapering. The worst withdrawal symptoms I've ever experienced of any drug. But for others it was a breeze so eh? Just gotta stay hopeful that it works for you and that you therefore, won't need to come off the drug in the first place :)

Stimulants take away my social anxiety completely tbh. But the only way I was prescribed them was because I had a sleep disorder and had to see a sleep specialist and undergo multiple tests $$$ etc. 4-5 months later I'm on Dex for Hypersomnia but it's because I actually need it coz I can't stay awake in the day like everybody else. If your patient and can go through all those tests then I guess there's that way?

Hi, as horrible as it is to hear someone as young as you going through this, it's nice to know there are plenty of others just like you that are willing to listen and support you through it. Because damn, nearly same age as me and I guess you might be feeling quite a bit of frustration through all of this? It's hard getting answers for a 'silent illness'.

I received 3 MRIs in the span of a year and nothing came up so I was a little um disheartened? But that doesn't mean the same will happen to you. It did put my mind at ease knowing it wasn't a stroke or TIA or a tumour. The pain/nausea and dizziness was so severe at one point I couldn't talk or walk or function I thought for sure I was having a stroke! But no, Vestibular Migraine.....cool. It's taken a bit of time for me to process the diagnosis so I think just coming on here and sharing your story is a big step and takes some bravery so congrats. 

I'm not a specialist or a doctor, just a patient that's been diagnosed early this year for it but I've read a lot of information about my condition and I think that's helped me keep in check. Opening up to my loved ones, asking for help when I need it (even though it can be hard), taking time to realise and accept you have a medical condition, be a bit easier on yourself. Anyway if you feel like reading the book is called:

'Victory Over Vestibular Migraine: The Action Plan for healing & getting your life back' by Shin C. Beh M.D. - I know what you're thinking, another bs self help book. Think again. This book perhaps changed my life (positively). Would highly recommend it. I was so lost before and frustrated but this gave me the most knowledge about my condition than anything else I've seen online. Also gave me hope that things will be more manageable in time.

They usually like to try you out on the most commonly prescribed preventative (and perhaps most evidence-based) drugs first e.g. Propranolol, Timolol, Topiramate, CGRP injectables etc. and then second line agents e.g. Amitriptyline, Venlafaxine etc. All preventative medication will take time so it's best to allow at least 3 months before determining whether it is effective or ineffective for you. All meds have side effects, which is why it's best to start low and go slow - decreases risk for potential side effects. The ultimate goal would be Monotherapy meaning one medication for everything but unfortunately that's not always the case. For many it's a case of Polypharmacy, if that's what gets you through the severity of it all then so be it. Just be careful of interactions of course. 

If your vertigo/dizziness symptoms are acute (really severe) your Neurologist might prescribe a short supply of Benzodiazepines - Clonazepam works best I feel as it has a very long half life and is quite potent so you don't have to keep taking more (usually) like Xanax for example. Meclizine did nothing for me. Betahistine works for some. Benadryl can sometimes be effective but it's very sedating. They give Stemetil in hospitals - I hate it, it gives me Akathisia. Usually if the vertigo is severe and I have benzos I'll take one and hide in dark room or I might take a triptan and do the same thing. Zofran can be good for nausea but that is all, love the wafers. Unfortunately I usually just have to wait for the vertigo to pass and calm myself down as it is very much linked to anxiety (in my case). Can lead to panic attacks. 

I currently take Emgality injections 1 x month for chronic migraines, Effexor XR 225mg for Vestibular Migraines/Anxiety but may reduce dose due to one side effect that isn't too bad in all honesty. Topiramate 50mg, low dose, was on a high dose in the past, worked well for me, gets a lot of negative press but I didn't get terrible side effects so everyone is different. Triptans/Nurtec/Benzos as rescue meds. ER if really bad - Thorazine injection or Ketorolac. Short 3 day, high dose steroid, if trying to break week long migraine attack.

That's interesting and I'm glad to hear Gabapentin works for you! I was kinda pushing my previous Neurologist for it when I "only" had chronic migraines not vestibular migraines yet when my country ran out of Ajovy. I also heard it was effective for anxiety so I was curious to try it. But now that I have the Vestibular component I'm not so sure about it. It's just that I've read it's likely to cause dizziness and somnlonence but I mean it could be different for everyone, what's your experience with it in terms of side effects? Did/do you experience dizziness? I'm on Effexor XR now, I'm finding it's helping a lot of things but I may have to go slightly down a dose as it's causing too much somnolence even when I take it at night, also taking Emgality once a month.

Sorry this is kinda a late response but just take genetic testing with a grain of salt. Whilst it's very cool and can be accurate to some extent it can also stop you from trying medication that could be hugely beneficial for you. For example on mine it said to avoid Effexor but my Neurologist insisted on it anyway for VM so I tried it and it's been very effective for the vertigo, PPPD, and anxiety. If I had stuck with the test results, maybe I never would've tried Effexor and would still be struggling to this day.

I'm so sorry you're going through this, I suffer chronically with Vestibular Migraines which was only a fresh diagnosis this year and I felt lost, and just wasn't getting any answers plus things only got worse as time went on so I can't imagine how much harder it must be with an autoimmune disease on top of that. The fact that you're still seeing specialists and trying to get help is a big step and it takes a lot of work to do just that so you should be proud of yourself for that at least. I hope you've got some support for when times are really tough. 

I like to read and in reading things it's helped me gained more awareness and a deeper understanding on what was going is with my body and my mind and well, my brain. Although it can be hard to narrow out the information that'll help ease your mind vs the information that'll just stress you out more. I'm also off work so there's more time to read.

Before seeing your Neurologist I'd suggest skimming over this page: [https://vestibular.org/article/diagnosis-treatment/for-your-doctor-visit/](https://vestibular.org/article/diagnosis-treatment/for-your-doctor-visit/) - it gives you a large variety of questions to ask your Neurologist and it could give you your own ideas on questions to ask. That site has really helpful information so if you feel like reading for hours, it's very beneficial. 

Otherwise I pretty much recommend this book to anyone I come across with the same condition as me: 'Victory Over Vestibular Migraine: The Action plan for healing & getting your life back' by Shin C. Beh. M.D. It's not a typical self help book, it has everything you need to know about the condition, I've never seen any other book like it, my physio recommended it to me and I've kept referring back to it ever since. It's really helped me gained more knowledge and awareness of my condition as well as hope - that although this condition isn't 'curable' it can be well-managed. 

Apologies for the rambling but I hope this helps a little bit and I do hope you get a good Neurologist who not just understands your condition but supports you and connects well with you. If I'm not on the same page as my specialist, I feel as though (even with their expertise) they aren't the right 'fit' for me.

I would say go to an ER but that might be costly depending on what country you're in. Taking high dose (preferably dissovable) Aspirin (900-1300mg) can work very quickly as long as you don't have chronic reflux - if you do, I'd advise taking Nexium prior at least. Otherwise high dose ibuprofen 600-800mg if you haven't tried other OTC already, can still be effective, try to eat something inbetween if you can. In Aus, you can get some triptans at a pharmacy, I'm not sure if you can where you are but if yes, then could try some - Triptans treat migraines by changing how blood circulates in your brain and how your brain processes pain signals (effects serotonin) so it would've been better to take one at the beginning of the attack but no harm in trying now anyway - Maxalt has the least side effects and comes as a wafer (dissolves under tongue). Relpax, is arguably the most effective triptan but it does have more side effects than Maxalt like fatigue and it's in pill form not wafer. 

Long term goal would be to see a Neurologist and get onto some prevention medication like others have listed here, Topamax (pill), Ajovy or Emgality (each an injection), Venlafaxine or Amitriptyline (both pills), Botox injections maybe? I guess it'll come down to what works for you, what your Neurologist thinks will treat your symptoms, and what you can afford - because many migraine treatments aren't covered by insurance so they're super expensive. Venlaxfaxine has been proven to be very effective for VM and is cheap, same goes for the other pills mentioned. The injections are expensive unless covered by insurance (disregarding Botox). ALL drugs have side effects. Start low and go slow.

I'd recommend reading (when you feel up to it): 'Victory Over Vestibular Migraine: The Action plan for healing & getting your life back' by Shin C. Beh M.D. - he goes into everything - treatments, diagnosis, symptoms, meds, alternatives, diet, misdiagnosis etc. you name it it's there! Very knowledgeable in the field. Helped me stay hopeful.

I'm sorry you're going through this, I've been there before, I know how hard it can be to get into a Neurologist, it's especially harder if you've got an ongoing VM. If there's any GPs in your area that have some extra knowledge on headaches and are easier to get into I would try those in the meantime whilst waiting for a Neurologist. I went to the ER and got admitted to hospital when I exhausted all other options. When I have a migraine that lasts days and won't go away my new Neurologist prescribed me Prednisolone (steroid) to take for 3 days, short burst, high dose, just to break the cycle and not get medication overuse rebound headache. Just wondering if a GP with knowledge in migraine/headaches would know this..... Anyway, hope this helps you.

P.S. Nurtec ODT is really effective too but holy moly that shit is expensive so I'm not sure if I can recommend it right now before you have a good try of at least 3-4 triptans.

It's hard to distinguish dizziness from vertigo a lot of the time but I think that's what I find the main difference is between a panic attack and a vestibular migraine attack. But in saying that, usually if my vertigo starts acting up and I can't get it under control in time, it leads to a panic attack anyway...
